extracted.intended_audience: trademark attorneys, IP practitioners, EUIPO examiners, brand owners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria applied by the EUIPO Boards (Grand Board) when assessing registrability, invalidity, revocation, conversion, proof-of-use and likelihood of confusion for European Union trade marks under the EUTM/EUTMR/CTMR framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective mark proprietor requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Articles 74 to 76 EUTMR, an EU collective mark must be capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the members of the proprietor association from those of other undertakings; in practice this requires an ownership and governance framework that is genuinely associative in nature, including meaningful member participation in the adoption and operation of the regulations governing use of the collective mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A public authority acting unilaterally cannot be proprietor of an EU collective mark (example: Diputación Provincial de Burgos). Examine ownership/governance to ensure genuine association and meaningful member participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish collective marks from certification marks / official guarantee risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective marks and certification marks serve different essential functions and must not be conflated; where a sign is likely to be perceived as an official guarantee or quality seal, particularly centred on geographical origin and administered unilaterally by a public body, the public may be misled and refusal under Article 76(2) EUTMR may be triggered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the public would view a sign as an official guarantee (quality/origin seal), treat it under certification/official-sign principles and consider refusal risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptiveness under Article 7(1)(c) EUTMR
rubrics_metrics.description: A sign is unregistrable where it may be used, in normal trade, to designate a characteristic of the goods or services; the list of characteristics is non-exhaustive and includes 'other characteristics' such as subject matter or content (e.g., recordings, publications, educational/entertainment services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suffices that descriptiveness exists in only part of the EU; assessment may be by reference to the relevant language community (e.g., English-speaking public including Ireland and Malta). Consider whether sign immediately and unequivocally indicates subject-matter or content of goods/services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptiveness implies lack of distinctive character (Article 7(1)(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sign is descriptive under Article 7(1)(c) EUTMR (e.g., indicates content/subject-matter), it is, by the same token, incapable of indicating commercial origin and is therefore devoid of distinctive character under Article 7(1)(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing distinctiveness, first check for descriptiveness; a direct descriptive relationship that allows the public to perceive content without further thought usually defeats distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public policy / morality refusal (Article 7(1)(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: A sign may be refused if it would offend a significant portion of the relevant public as contrary to human dignity or accepted principles of morality; assessment focuses on whether the term is offensive to persons of normal levels of tolerance and sensitivity who come into contact with the sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant identity, membership of offended group, or anti-homophobia commitments are irrelevant; consider social consensus and evidence showing offence. Examples: homophobic slurs, trivialising pandemic references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of expression balancing for Article 7(1)(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 7(1)(f) is a valid limitation of freedom of expression (Article 11(2) Charter in conjunction with Article 52(1) Charter); freedom of commercial expression must be balanced against the need to protect the public from offensive language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply proportionality: interference must be necessary and less restrictive than an outright ban on use; weigh applicant's expression rights against public interest in protecting moral values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehabilitation / reappropriation evidence for offensive terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence must demonstrate that an offensive expression has been rehabilitated or reappropriated; absent such evidence, the expression remains offensive to a significant part of the public and refusal under Article 7(1)(f) follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess submitted socio-linguistic evidence; if evidence fails to show reappropriation, treat term as still offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion possible despite non-final refusal (Articles 66(1),71(3),139)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversion cannot be excluded on the basis of a decision refusing the EUTM application in ex parte or inter partes proceedings where the application is subsequently withdrawn before the refusal could take effect (i.e., during the appeal period), even if no appeal is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conversion is requested after withdrawal during appeal period, examine timing and whether earlier (non-final) refusal had taken legal effect; conversion may remain possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion after withdrawal (Article 139(5)) and applicability of Article 139(2)(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where conversion is requested subsequent to a withdrawal of the EUTM application (Article 139(5)), Article 139(2)(b) EUTMR does not apply; EU-27 conversion can remain possible even if EUIPO previously determined a (non-final) obstacle in part of the EU.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different statutory paths apply depending on withdrawal vs timing; examine the specific conversion provisions and past Office determinations carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 7(1)(f) scope — prevention of administrative assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 7(1)(f) EUTMR is not limited to trade marks whose use would be prohibited; organs of public administration should not positively assist those who wish to further business aims by using trade marks contrary to basic values of civilised society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and registries must consider whether registration itself would amount to assistance in promoting marks contrary to accepted moral values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptiveness assessment of regional/local language terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A term in a locally-spoken language should be denied registration under Article 7(1)(c) if it is the name of the goods, if it is used to describe features of the goods, or if it would be reasonable for such an association to be established in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restrict 'relevant public' too narrowly; consider likelihood of association arising and future reasonable associations, even for names of local artefacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country names and geographical indications (Article 7(1)(c) / Article 59)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mark containing the name of a country will be perceived by the relevant public as indicating that the goods/services originate from that country, or it is reasonable to assume it will be so associated; such marks are descriptive of the goods/services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess perception by relevant public and evidence of established geographic link; consider descriptiveness and potential invalidity under territorial-origin rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner revision and reopening of proceedings (Article 69)
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may lawfully, after granting revision, reopen the proceeding and adopt a new decision after having heard the applicant; subsequent grant of revision does not preclude reopening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where revision is granted, procedural fairness requires opportunity to be heard before any new decision; check Article 69 and procedural timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine use standard: EU revocation vs national conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: In revocation (non-use) proceedings the applicable standard is Article 58(1)(a) EUTMR — the single autonomous EU concept of genuine use; in conversion requests the applicable standard is the national legal framework on genuine use governed by the law of the Member State for which conversion is requested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A final revocation decision under EU law does not produce res judicata effect in conversion proceedings because different substantive law applies; conversion applicant bears burden to prove evidence would be considered genuine use under the relevant national law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of use request must be a 'separate document' (Article 10(1) EUTMDR)
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement to submit a request for proof of use as a 'separate document' does not necessarily mean a separate file/envelope, but the request must be presented separately (e.g., as a distinct submission or as a separate annex); merging it into observations may render it inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate section titles within a continuous submission with continuous pagination may be insufficient; signature covering whole submission does not cure non-compliance. Ensure requests for proof of use are clearly and separately presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness of purely figurative/ornamental marks
rubrics_metrics.description: A purely figurative sign that will be perceived first and foremost as an ornamental feature of the products (e.g., simple geometric pattern repeated) may be devoid of distinctive character because it is perceived as a mere decorative/pattern element rather than indicating trade origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the figurative design is an ornamental/pattern feature; simple geometric repetition is likely non-distinctive for surface-decorative applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter-signs and conceptual identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs perceived as a letter of the alphabet can convey the generic concept of that letter, but the mere fact that the same letter might describe both signs is not sufficient to establish conceptual identity or similarity — full semantic content must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When letters are stylised, regard the overall visual, aural, and conceptual impression; even if some see a letter, visual/aural differences can still prevent similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood of confusion assessment factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Likelihood of confusion depends on the comparison of the signs (visual, aural, conceptual), the similarity of goods/services (identity, similarity, complementarity), and the degree of attention of the relevant public; partial similarity of goods may produce partial upholding of opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider context (retail channels, supermarket sections), consumer attention (average, low, specialised), and relevant territories and language communities when comparing goods and signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due cause / legitimate descriptive use defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a generic or descriptive word element for an informative purpose (e.g., indicating presence of spa facilities) can amount to due cause and may negate claims of unfair advantage or likelihood of confusion with an earlier mark's reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the element performs an informative purpose and whether it takes undue advantage of an earlier mark; if clearly descriptive and used to inform consumers, due cause may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptiveness under Article 7(1)(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mark that entails a sufficiently serious risk of deceiving the public as to the nature, quality or geographical origin of the goods/services is unregistrable under Article 7(1)(g); the identity of the applicant is irrelevant to that assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess objective risk that consumers will be misled (e.g., geographic indications claiming origin that is false).

rubrics_metrics.name: Res judicata effect of General Court judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the General Court has decided a point by final judgment, the Grand Board considers itself bound by that reasoning as far as the same legal question is concerned (res judicata).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If issue already decided by GC, treat that outcome as binding on same question; however, new facts/evidence may allow re-examination on ancillary matters (e.g., acquired distinctiveness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired distinctiveness (Article 7(3) / evidence requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of distinctiveness acquired through use must be substantiated; the Board may remit the case to the Cancellation Division solely to examine acquired distinctiveness if required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide robust evidence of market exposure, duration, geographic scope, nature of use within the Community; isolated declarations or attendance lists without detailed provenance are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking account of actual use versions and graphical representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Following case-law (e.g., Court T-20/16 and T-124/20), the version in which a sign is actually used may not be taken into account if it differs from the graphic representation on the register; distinctiveness must be assessed on the graphic representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant tries to rely on use of a variant of the registered depiction, examination may be limited to the registered graphic; consider remittal where acquired distinctiveness based on the used version is alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant public and territory determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'relevant public' can be general consumers or specialised publics depending on the goods/services and language community (e.g., English-speaking public, specialists outside the medical sector); the territory is typically the whole EU unless specific evidence justifies limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the relevant linguistic communities and consumer profiles (average, specialised) and apply the appropriate degree of attention and perception standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use outside the Community not prima facie sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of use in third countries (outside the Community) is not sufficient to show use in the Community; the applicant must prove effective use inside the Community in the same fashion as claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete proof of Community use (sales, advertising, geographic spread) rather than attendance by Community nationals at events abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation of evidence / belated substantiation (CTMIR Rule 20/Rule 19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission of translations of earlier rights after the expiry of time limits generally results in rejection of the opposition with no discretion to accept late translations; substantiation of earlier marks is a preliminary matter that must be settled before deciding the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate and submit substantiating documents within specified time-limits; late translations are normally inadmissible and can be fatal to oppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence after appeal filed — examiner revocation limits (Article 61 CTMR)
rubrics_metrics.description: After a notice of appeal is filed, jurisdiction lies solely with the Boards of Appeal; an examiner may only rectify within narrow conditions of Article 61 CTMR and a later unilateral revocation contrary to Article 61 is null and void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If appeal is pending, examiners should not issue new decisions that attempt to revoke or replace contested decisions outside Article 61 procedure; such acts risk nullity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional shape exclusion from registration (Article 7(1)(e)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-dimensional shape must be precluded from registration as a trade mark if its essential functional characteristics are attributable solely to the technical result (i.e., functional features necessary for product utility), even if the result could be achieved by other shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the shape's dominant features serve purely functional/technical purposes (example: Lego brick studs); if so, refuse under the functional exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof & sufficiency of evidence for use/acquired distinctiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants bear the burden to prove genuine use or acquired distinctiveness; proof must show duration, intensity, nature, and geographic scope of use in the Community — limited or weak evidence (e.g., small numbers of statements) will not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide comprehensive documentary evidence (sales figures, advertising, market share, distribution evidence) and demonstrate perception by a substantial part of the relevant public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict application of procedural deadlines (statutory time-limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time-limits (e.g., four-month time-limit for statement of grounds; one-month for translations) are strict and not suspendable; failure to comply leads to inadmissibility or dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe statutory deadlines exactly; do not rely on later curing or mutual agreement to suspend time-limits.
